title: What must staff know under Australia's Scams Prevention Framework?
description: Scams Prevention Framework governance duties for banks, telcos and digital platforms, the 2026 and 2027 start dates, and where training awaits codes.
shortAnswer: The Scams Prevention Framework, inserted as Part IVF of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 in February 2025, requires regulated banks, telecommunications providers and digital platforms to document and implement scam governance, have a senior officer certify it annually, and take reasonable steps to prevent, detect, report, disrupt and respond to scams. The Act contains no express staff training duty. As at November 2026, training detail awaits the sector codes, which the government is still developing.
keyTakeaways: The Scams Prevention Framework Act 2025 (No. 15, 2025) received assent on February 20, 2025 and inserted Part IVF into the Competition and Consumer Act 2010.
Regulated entities had to join the Australian Financial Complaints Authority from September 1, 2026; most obligations apply from March 31, 2027.

Section 58BD requires documented and implemented governance policies, procedures, metrics and targets; section 58BE requires senior officer certification within 12 months of becoming regulated and annually after that.

Governance breaches are tier 2 contraventions; breaches of the prevent, detect, disrupt and respond principles are tier 1, with a corporate maximum of the greater of 159,745 penalty units, three times the benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover.

The Act does not mention staff training for regulated entities. Sector codes may set governance content and reasonable steps, and courts can order an education and training program after a contravention.
regulator: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) as SPF general regulator, with ASIC (banks) and ACMA (telecommunications) as sector regulators
appliesTo: Entities providing regulated services in the banking sector, regulated by ASIC as sector regulator
Telecommunications providers providing regulated services, regulated by ACMA as sector regulator
Digital platforms providing regulated services, regulated by the ACCC as sector regulator
Senior officers who certify governance, and staff who handle scam reports, investigations and complaints

sections.heading: What is the Scams Prevention Framework and when does it apply?

blocks.text: The Scams Prevention Framework (SPF) is a principles based regime that makes designated sectors legally responsible for combating scams on their services. The [Scams Prevention Framework Act 2025](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2025A00015/asmade/text), assented to on February 20, 2025, inserted Part IVF into the Competition and Consumer Act 2010. The ACCC's [SPF page](https://www.accc.gov.au/about-us/scams-prevention-framework) says entities in banking, telecommunications and digital platforms "will be required by law to take action to prevent, detect, disrupt, report, and respond to scams".

blocks.title: Status as at November 2026
blocks.text: The governance, prevent, detect, report, disrupt and respond principles are in the Act, but the sector SPF codes and most SPF rules are not yet final. Training requirements specific to staff, if any, will depend on those instruments. Check the ACCC's SPF page and the Federal Register of Legislation before relying on any date.

sections.heading: Does the Scams Prevention Framework require staff training?

blocks.text: Not expressly. The Act's only references to training concern the qualifications of regulators' inspectors and delegates, and a court's power to order a training program after a contravention. No provision of the SPF principles tells a regulated entity to train its staff, and no training hours, topics or frequencies are set.

Training is nonetheless the practical way to meet several duties. Section 58BB says whether an entity has taken "reasonable steps" depends on its size, the kind of services, its consumer base, the scam risks those services face, and compliance with any relevant SPF code obligations, which must be the primary consideration where they apply. Section 58BH allows each sector's SPF code to specify what entities must include in their governance policies and procedures, which is where sector specific training content would most likely appear. Until codes are made, entities should treat training as part of the governance arrangements they document under section 58BD rather than as a standalone requirement.

After a breach, training can become mandatory. Section 58FZO allows a court to make a probation order of up to 3 years, which may direct a person "to establish a compliance program, or an education and training program" for employees and others involved in the business, designed to ensure awareness of their responsibilities.

sections.heading: What are the SPF governance obligations?

blocks.text: SPF principle 1 requires each regulated entity to document, implement, measure, certify and evidence its scam governance. The obligations are civil penalty provisions in Subdivision B of Division 2 of Part IVF.

items: **Section 58BD:** document governance policies and procedures about preventing, detecting and disrupting scams, responding to scams, and reports relating to scams; implement them; and develop and implement performance metrics and targets that measure their effectiveness.

**Section 58BE:** a senior officer must certify in writing whether the governance policies, procedures, metrics and targets comply, within 12 months of the entity becoming regulated and within 7 days after each 12 month anniversary. A senior officer is an officer or senior manager within the meaning of the Corporations Act 2001.
**Section 58BF:** keep records of material information about each documenting, implementation and senior officer consideration of those arrangements for at least 6 years.
**Section 58BG:** give the regulator copies of the governance documents or records within 10 business days of a written request, or a longer period allowed.
**Section 58BH:** the sector SPF code may set what governance policies must include and the factors entities must consider.

blocks.text: Under section 58AK, acts done in relation to an agent acting within its authority are taken to be done in relation to the regulated entity, so outsourced contact centers and fraud operations need to be covered by the same governance and capability arrangements.

sections.heading: Which operational duties will frontline and fraud staff carry out?

blocks.text: Staff in fraud, contact center and complaints roles will execute the five operational principles, several of which run on fixed clocks. The table maps each principle to the roles most involved and the evidence a regulator could test. The role and evidence columns are an original, illustrative analysis; the obligations and section numbers come from the Act.

blocks.text: Section 58AI defines actionable scam intelligence objectively: an entity has it when there are "reasonable grounds for the entity to suspect" that an activity using its service is a scam, and the Act notes that information provided by consumers, including complaints, may be relevant. That makes frontline recognition and escalation a capability the governance procedures need to address. Internal dispute resolution under the respond principle sits alongside ASIC's existing IDR standard, covered on the [RG 271 complaints training page](/regulations/asic-rg-271-complaints-handling-training).

sections.heading: What penalties apply for breaching the SPF?

blocks.text: Penalties are set in two tiers. Under section 58FK, tier 1 covers the prevent, detect, disrupt and respond principles (Subdivisions C, D, F and G): the maximum for a body corporate is the greater of 159,745 penalty units, three times the benefit obtained, or 30% of adjusted turnover during the breach turnover period, and 7,990 penalty units for other persons. Under section 58FL, tier 2 covers governance and reporting (Subdivisions B and E) and SPF code provisions: the greater of 31,950 penalty units, three times the benefit, or 10% of adjusted turnover, and 1,600 penalty units for other persons.

At the $364 penalty unit value the ACCC's [fines and penalties page](https://www.accc.gov.au/business/compliance-and-enforcement/fines-and-penalties) reports from July 1, 2026, the fixed amounts equal about $58.1 million for tier 1 and about $11.6 million for tier 2 for a body corporate. The ACCC's [2026-27 compliance and enforcement priorities](https://www.accc.gov.au/about-us/accc-strategy-and-priorities/compliance-and-enforcement-priorities) state that it "will enforce the Scams Protection Framework" (the ACCC's wording).

sections.heading: How should regulated entities prepare their people before the codes are final?

blocks.text: Entities can build the capability layer now around the duties already in the Act, and adjust content when codes and rules are made. A practical sequence:

items: Map each section 58BD governance procedure to the roles that perform it, using the method in [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).
Brief the senior officers who will give section 58BE certifications on what they are certifying and the records section 58BF requires.

Train frontline and contact center staff to recognize and escalate reports and complaints that may amount to actionable scam intelligence, so the 28 day investigation clock in section 58BN can be met.
Train IDR staff on the scam complaint pathway and AFCA's role from March 31, 2027.

Record content versions so training can be revised quickly once sector codes specify governance content or reasonable steps; see [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

blocks.text: Banks should align this work with existing obligations covered on the [Banking Code of Practice](/regulations/banking-code-of-practice-staff-training) and [AUSTRAC AML/CTF training](/regulations/austrac-aml-ctf-training-requirements) pages, and telecommunications providers with the consumer contact rules on the [ACMA spam and telemarketing](/regulations/acma-spam-and-telemarketing-compliance-training) page.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the SPF principles, sections and roles as a structured framework, so each governance procedure is linked to the roles that perform it and the assessment points they must demonstrate. When sector codes and SPF rules are made, the new provisions are added to the framework and the affected roles and assessments are identified directly, rather than by rereading every course.

faqs.q: Which businesses does the Scams Prevention Framework cover?
faqs.a: The ACCC says entities providing regulated services in the banking, telecommunications and digital platforms sectors. The ACCC points to the Treasury website for which specific services are designated. Each sector has a sector regulator: ASIC for banks, ACMA for telecommunications providers and the ACCC for digital platforms, with the ACCC also acting as general regulator.

faqs.q: Is there a mandatory scams training course for bank or telco staff?
faqs.a: Not under the Act as at November 2026. The SPF principles contain no express training obligation. Sector SPF codes, still being developed, may specify governance content or reasonable steps that imply training, and a court can order an education and training program under section 58FZO after a contravention.

faqs.q: What does the senior officer certify each year?
faqs.a: Under section 58BE, a senior officer must certify in writing whether the entity's SPF governance policies, procedures, metrics and targets comply with the governance subdivision. The first certification is due within 12 months of becoming a regulated entity, then within 7 days after each 12 month anniversary.

faqs.q: How long must SPF governance records be kept?
faqs.a: At least 6 years. Section 58BF requires records of material information about each documenting and revision of the governance arrangements, each implementation, each senior officer consideration including certification, and any other activity prescribed by the SPF rules.
